title: The Dilemma of Statistical Parity: Blind Spots in Measuring Disparate Impact
text:
Relying solely on Disparate Impact (DI) metrics risks adopting a functionalist definition of fairness—one that prioritizes mathematical parity over true equity. While DI provides a necessary quantitative check for identifying statistical disparities across protected groups, focusing too heavily on achieving acceptable ratios can serve as an ethical blind spot.

The primary moral dilemma lies in assuming that removing correlation bias guarantees equitable outcomes. Achieving equal predictive accuracy or selection rates merely mandates procedural fairness without addressing the deeper systemic causes of inequality. Such over-reliance might lead developers to mistakenly believe compliance with a metric absolves them of responsibility for disparate real-world consequences.

Responsible deployment requires understanding that metrics like DI are indicators, not ultimate measures of justice. They guide auditing processes but must be paired with qualitative human rights assessments and context-specific impact studies to prevent the superficial appearance of neutrality from masking structural unfairness.
